# Team Retrospective Board Web App

## Summary

Build a lightweight web application that helps software teams run recurring sprint retrospectives. The app should allow a facilitator to create a retro session, teammates to add cards under columns like "Went Well", "To Improve", and "Actions", and then collaborate in real time to group, vote, and track action items.

## Goals

- Make it very fast to spin up a new retro, invite the team, and capture feedback.
- Keep the UI simple enough that non-technical users can use it without training.
- Support fully remote teams working from different locations.

## Core Features

### 1. Session Management
- A facilitator can create a new retro session with:
  - A title (e.g. "Sprint 24 Retro")
  - An optional description
  - A date/time (default to now)
- The system generates a shareable link (URL) for the session.
- No login is required for basic usage, but sessions should have a random, hard-to-guess ID.

### 2. Columns & Cards
- Default columns: "Went Well", "To Improve", "Questions", "Actions".
- The facilitator can rename, add, or remove columns.
- Any participant can add cards to any column with:
  - Short text (1–3 sentences)
  - Optional author name or initials
- Cards can be edited or deleted by the person who created them (or by the facilitator).

### 3. Grouping & Voting
- Participants can drag and drop cards to reorder them or move them between columns.
- Cards can be grouped into clusters (e.g. "Deployment issues").
  - A cluster has a title and contains one or more cards.
- Each participant has a limited number of votes per session (configurable, default 5).
- Voting rules:
  - A participant can assign multiple votes to the same card/cluster or spread votes across several.
  - The UI shows the current vote count per card/cluster.

### 4. Action Items
- From any card or cluster, the facilitator can create an "Action Item" with:
  - Title
  - Description
  - Owner (free-text or simple dropdown of known participants)
  - Due date (optional)
- Action items appear in a separate, always-visible list.
- Action items can be marked as done and edited later.

### 5. Real-Time Collaboration
- Changes to cards, votes, and action items should appear in near real time for all connected participants.
- If real-time sync is temporarily unavailable, the app should still work for a single user and sync changes when connection is restored.

## Non-Goals (Nice to Have Later)

These are explicitly **not required** for the first version but should be kept in mind when designing the system:

- Authentication and user accounts.
- Persistent team workspaces and history of all retros per team.
- Exporting data to Jira, Trello, or other tools.

## Technical Constraints

- Build as a single-page web application.
- Should run in all modern browsers.
- Back-end and database choice is flexible; a simple implementation using a hosted database or file-based store is acceptable for now.

components.name: React SPA
components.description: Single‑page application that renders the retro board, handles drag‑and‑drop, voting UI and communicates with the backend via REST and WebSocket.

components.name: Express REST API
components.description: Stateless HTTP layer exposing CRUD endpoints for sessions, columns, cards, clusters and action items.

components.name: Socket.io Hub
components.description: WebSocket server that pushes state changes (card moves, votes, new action items) to all connected clients and persists events to the database.

components.name: PostgreSQL
components.description: Relational store for sessions, columns, cards, clusters, votes and action items. Chosen for ACID guarantees and simple relational queries.

architecture.dataFlow: 1. The facilitator opens the React SPA and creates a session via a POST to the Express REST API. The API writes the session row to PostgreSQL and returns a random UUID link. 2. All participants load the SPA using the shared URL; the SPA opens a WebSocket connection to the Socket.io Hub and subscribes to the session ID. 3. When a user adds/edits/moves a card, the SPA sends a REST request (for persistence) and emits a Socket.io event. The Hub writes the change to PostgreSQL and broadcasts the event to every connected client, which updates its local UI. 4. Voting and clustering follow the same pattern – REST for durability, WebSocket for immediate UI sync. 5. If the WebSocket disconnects, the SPA falls back to REST‑only mode; once the connection restores, it re‑synchronizes missing events by re‑fetching the session state.
integrations: Optional CDN for static assets (e.g., Cloudflare)
nonFunctional: Scalability – Stateless Express API and Socket.io allow horizontal scaling behind a load balancer; PostgreSQL can be scaled read‑replicas if needed.
Security – Random UUID session IDs, CORS whitelist, input validation, rate limiting on API endpoints.
Observability – Structured JSON logs (pino), health‑check endpoint, basic request metrics via Prometheus exporter.
Fault tolerance – Automatic reconnection logic in the SPA, idempotent REST endpoints, database transaction safety.
Performance – Minimal payloads, selective broadcasting (only to clients in the same session), indexes on session_id columns.

techStack.rationale: React has the largest ecosystem, mature drag‑and‑drop libraries (react‑beautiful‑dnd), and TypeScript support that eases future maintenance. Vite provides fast dev server start‑up. Vue and Svelte are viable but would require additional learning for a team already familiar with React.

Express is ultra‑lightweight, matches the simplicity of the app, and integrates seamlessly with Socket.io. Fastify offers better performance but adds a learning curve for middleware patterns; NestJS brings a full‑blown framework that is overkill for a single service.

Socket.io abstracts reconnection, fallback transports and room management, which speeds development of per‑session broadcasting. Raw ws requires manual handling of these concerns. Firebase would introduce external vendor lock‑in and unnecessary cost for a simple board.

PostgreSQL gives relational integrity for sessions, cards, votes and supports complex queries (e.g., ordering, aggregation). Supabase provides a managed instance with zero‑ops backups, fitting the "simple implementation" constraint. SQLite would limit concurrent users and lacks built‑in HA; MongoDB is document‑oriented and would require extra modeling for relational constraints.

Docker guarantees environment parity across dev and prod while keeping the deployment footprint tiny (one container). Render offers free tier, automatic HTTPS and simple scaling without managing Kubernetes. Heroku is similar but pricing is higher for comparable resources; Elastic Beanstalk adds unnecessary AWS complexity.

GitHub Actions integrates directly with the repository, provides free minutes for open‑source, and can run lint, unit tests, build Docker image and push to Render. GitLab CI would require moving the repo; CircleCI adds external service overhead.

techStack.choice: Jest + React Testing Library for frontend, Supertest for API
techStack.rationale: Jest is the de‑facto standard for unit testing in React/TS projects, offers fast watch mode and built‑in coverage. React Testing Library encourages testing from the user’s perspective. Supertest pairs nicely with Express for HTTP integration tests. Mocha is older and lacks the same ecosystem; Cypress is great for e2e but not needed for unit coverage at this stage.
pino is extremely low‑overhead and outputs structured JSON, making it easy to ship to any log aggregation service. Winston is more feature‑rich but slower; Log4js is less actively maintained.

dbDesign.rationale: PostgreSQL provides strong ACID guarantees, rich relational features, JSON support for complex queries, and is already selected in the tech stack (Supabase managed PostgreSQL). It scales with read replicas and supports the transactional consistency needed for real‑time board operations.

sampleQueries.description: Fetch the complete board state for a given session, including ordered columns, clusters, and cards (JSON nested structure).
sampleQueries.sql:
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
  'session_id', s.id,
  'title', s.title,
  'columns', jsonb_agg(
    jsonb_build_object(
      'id', c.id,
      'title', c.title,
      'position', c.position,
      'clusters', (
        SELECT jsonb_agg(
          jsonb_build_object(
            'id', cl.id,
            'title', cl.title,
            'position', cl.position,
            'cards', (
              SELECT jsonb_agg(
                jsonb_build_object(
                  'id', cr.id,
                  'content', cr.content,
                  'author_name', cr.author_name,
                  'position', cr.position,
                  'vote_count', (
                    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM votes v WHERE v.target_type = 'card' AND v.target_id = cr.id
                  )
                )
                ORDER BY cr.position
              )
              FROM cards cr
              WHERE cr.cluster_id = cl.id
            )
          )
          ORDER BY cl.position
        )
        FROM clusters cl
        WHERE cl.column_id = c.id
      ),
      'cards_without_cluster', (
        SELECT jsonb_agg(
          jsonb_build_object(
            'id', cr.id,
            'content', cr.content,
            'author_name', cr.author_name,
            'position', cr.position,
            'vote_count', (
              SELECT COUNT(*) FROM votes v WHERE v.target_type = 'card' AND v.target_id = cr.id
            )
          )
          ORDER BY cr.position
        )
        FROM cards cr
        WHERE cr.column_id = c.id AND cr.cluster_id IS NULL
      )
    )
    ORDER BY c.position
  )
) AS board_state
FROM sessions s
JOIN columns c ON c.session_id = s.id
WHERE s.id = '<<SESSION_UUID>>'
GROUP BY s.id, s.title;

sampleQueries.description: Get top 5 cards with the highest vote count in a session.
sampleQueries.sql:
SELECT cr.id, cr.content, cr.author_name, COUNT(v.id) AS vote_count
FROM cards cr
LEFT JOIN votes v ON v.target_type = 'card' AND v.target_id = cr.id
WHERE cr.session_id = '<<SESSION_UUID>>'
GROUP BY cr.id, cr.content, cr.author_name
ORDER BY vote_count DESC, cr.position ASC
LIMIT 5;

sampleQueries.description: Count how many votes a particular voter has used in a session (to enforce limit).
List all open action items for a session with their source (card or cluster) details.
sampleQueries.sql:
SELECT ai.id, ai.source_type, ai.source_id, ai.owner_name, ai.due_date, ai.description, ai.status,
       CASE ai.source_type
         WHEN 'card' THEN (SELECT jsonb_build_object('id', c.id, 'content', c.content) FROM cards c WHERE c.id = ai.source_id)
         WHEN 'cluster' THEN (SELECT jsonb_build_object('id', cl.id, 'title', cl.title) FROM clusters cl WHERE cl.id = ai.source_id)
       END AS source_detail
FROM action_items ai
WHERE ai.session_id = '<<SESSION_UUID>>' AND ai.status = 'open';

migrations.content:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "pgcrypto"; 

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sessions (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  title text NOT NULL,
  description text,
  scheduled_date date,
  vote_limit_per_user int NOT NULL DEFAULT 3,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TRIGGER set_timestamp_sessions
BEFORE UPDATE ON sessions
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION set_timestamp();

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS action_items (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  session_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES sessions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  source_type text NOT NULL CHECK (source_type IN ('card','cluster')),
  source_id uuid NOT NULL,
  owner_name text,
  due_date date,
  description text,
  status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open' CHECK (status IN ('open','done')),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (session_id, source_type, source_id)
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_action_items_session_status ON action_items (session_id, status);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_action_items_source ON action_items (source_type, source_id);

CREATE TRIGGER set_timestamp_action_items
BEFORE UPDATE ON action_items
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION set_timestamp();

userStories.soThat: participants can join the session without authentication
acceptanceCriteria: Given the facilitator fills title/description/date and clicks create, a session is persisted in the database and a UUID link is returned

userStories.iWant: to join a session via the shareable UUID link without logging in
acceptanceCriteria: When a participant opens the UUID link, the SPA loads the session data without requiring authentication
The participant sees the board with default columns and can interact with it

userStories.iWant: to view default columns and add cards with optional author information
userStories.soThat: I can share feedback during the retro
acceptanceCriteria: Participants can see default columns and add a card; the new card appears instantly in the UI
The new card is persisted in the database and is visible to other participants after refresh or via real‑time update

userStories.iWant: to rename, add, or delete columns on the board
userStories.soThat: the board fits the team’s needs for the retro
acceptanceCriteria: Facilitator can rename an existing column, add a new column, or delete a column; changes persist and are reflected for all participants
Deleting a column either removes its cards or prompts the facilitator to reassign them

userStories.iWant: to edit or delete the cards I created
userStories.soThat: I can correct mistakes or remove my input
acceptanceCriteria: Card creator can edit the card text and author; changes persist and are shown to all participants
Card creator can delete their own card; the card disappears for all participants

userStories.iWant: all session changes to be broadcast in near real time to every connected participant
acceptanceCriteria: When any user creates, moves, or edits a card, all other connected clients see the change within 200ms
Socket.io events are emitted for each change and correctly update client state

userStories.iWant: the app to automatically reconnect and replay missed events after a WebSocket disconnect
userStories.soThat: my view stays in sync without duplicate updates
acceptanceCriteria: If a client loses the WebSocket connection and later reconnects, it receives the latest session state and any missed events
No duplicate events are applied after reconnection

userStories.iWant: to vote on cards or clusters with a limited number of votes per session
acceptanceCriteria: Each participant can allocate up to the configured number of votes per session
Vote counts are displayed on cards/clusters and update in real time for all participants

userStories.iWant: to group related cards into clusters with a title
userStories.soThat: the board stays organized and themes emerge
acceptanceCriteria: Users can create a cluster, give it a title, and drag multiple cards into it

userStories.iWant: to convert any card or cluster into an action item with owner, due date, and description
userStories.soThat: action items are tracked and assigned
acceptanceCriteria: Facilitator can convert a card/cluster into an action item and specify title, description, owner, and optional due date

userStories.iWant: to view the list of action items and mark them as done
userStories.soThat: the team can see progress on follow‑up tasks
acceptanceCriteria: Participants can see all action items in a persistent side list
Marking an item as done updates its status instantly for all participants

userStories.iWant: the SPA to continue working via REST when the WebSocket connection drops and automatically resynchronize when it is restored
userStories.soThat: no work is lost during temporary connectivity issues
acceptanceCriteria: While WebSocket is disconnected, users can add/edit cards and the operations succeed via REST calls
When the connection is restored, the client syncs pending changes and the UI reflects the final state without loss

userStories.iWant: all components (session management, board, real‑time, voting, action items) wired together in the main application entry point
userStories.soThat: the retro board is fully functional end‑to‑end
acceptanceCriteria: Starting the application launches both the frontend SPA and the backend API, serving the SPA and exposing REST and WebSocket endpoints
A user can create a session, add cards, vote, create action items, and see all changes in real time without errors

comments.body: The `scripts` section contains duplicate keys (`dev`, `build`, `start`, `test`) and is missing a comma after the first `"test": "jest"`.
